specvec

species and communities as points in one space

specvec learns vectors for plant species and for vegetation plots from a table of which species occur in which plots, and with how much cover.

Each species becomes a point in a space of a few dozen dimensions, computed by a sparse eigendecomposition (Matrix and RSpectra) of a cover-weighted co-occurrence table. These species vectors are the embedding: species that keep the same company across plots sit close together. Each plot is placed in the same space as the cover-weighted average of its species’ vectors, so you can find a species’ ecological partners, compare plots with each other, and decide which plots or species to examine as unusual or changing.

specvec supports:

  • Cover-weighted co-occurrence. In the default method, abund_pmi, each plot two species share contributes the geometric mean of their covers, so a pair that dominates a plot weighs more than a pair where one species is a trace. Percent, proportion and Braun-Blanquet cover scales are read directly.
  • Community vectors. community_embedding() places plots beside the species; community_similarity() compares plots and community_novelty() scores a plot’s distance to a reference set.
  • Change through time. Embeddings computed per time window share one fixed frame, so species_trajectory() and community_trajectory() follow species and plots through time, and integration_trajectory() tracks a neophyte’s distance to the native community.
  • Comparing embedding methods. compare_embeddings() scores correspondence analysis, pointwise mutual information (PMI), cover-weighted PMI and GloVe on your own data under one fixed protocol.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/specvec")

The core methods need only Matrix and RSpectra. text2vec is needed only for the glove method, and FNN only to speed up nearest-neighbour queries.

Usage

  1. Build the data object from a long plot-species table with specvec().
  2. Learn the species vectors with species_embedding().
  3. Query a species’ neighbours with nearest_species().
  4. Place the plots in the same space with community_embedding().
library(specvec)

records <- data.frame(
  plot    = rep(c("p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "p5", "p6"), each = 3),
  species = c("Acer campestre", "Sambucus nigra", "Prunus avium",
              "Acer campestre", "Sambucus nigra", "Euonymus europaeus",
              "Acer campestre", "Prunus avium", "Euonymus europaeus",
              "Salix alba", "Humulus lupulus", "Sambucus nigra",
              "Salix alba", "Humulus lupulus", "Impatiens glandulifera",
              "Salix alba", "Impatiens glandulifera", "Humulus lupulus"),
  cover   = c(40, 10, 20, 55, 15, 10, 30, 25, 5,
              60, 20, 5, 50, 30, 25, 45, 35, 10)
)

x   <- specvec(records, plot = "plot", species = "species",
               abundance = "cover")
emb <- species_embedding(x, dim = 2, min_occurrence = 1)
nearest_species(emb, "Acer campestre")
#>                  species  similarity
#> 1           Prunus avium  0.99997356
#> 2     Euonymus europaeus  0.99983016
#> 3         Sambucus nigra  0.95937182
#> 4        Humulus lupulus  0.09946688
#> 5             Salix alba  0.06351129
#> 6 Impatiens glandulifera -0.05260996

The first three plots hold woodland-edge shrubs and trees, the last three a willow and riparian herbs, with Sambucus nigra in both groups. The neighbours of Acer campestre are the other woodland-edge species, with cosine similarity close to 1, followed by Sambucus nigra and then the riparian species near 0. The defaults, 64 dimensions and at least 5 plots per species, are set for full surveys; this example lowers both because it has six plots.

The input is a long table with one row per plot-species record. The plot and species columns are named in the call, and a cover column is optional; without it the weighting uses presence only. Preparing data and cover scales covers the cover scales, duplicate records and time columns.

comm <- community_embedding(x, embedding = emb)
round(community_similarity(comm), 2)
#>      p1   p2   p3   p4   p5   p6
#> p1 1.00 1.00 1.00 0.18 0.09 0.07
#> p2 1.00 1.00 1.00 0.20 0.11 0.08
#> p3 1.00 1.00 1.00 0.14 0.05 0.02
#> p4 0.18 0.20 0.14 1.00 1.00 0.99
#> p5 0.09 0.11 0.05 1.00 1.00 1.00
#> p6 0.07 0.08 0.02 0.99 1.00 1.00

The plot vectors fall into the same two groups: plots 1 to 3 are similar to each other and dissimilar to plots 4 to 6.

Neighbours of three neophytes in European vegetation

Fitted on a sample of 10,000 plots of European vegetation, the nearest neighbours of three established neophytes are species of the communities each one grows in. Robinia pseudoacacia is a nitrogen-fixing tree of dry, nutrient-rich woodland edges, and its neighbours are hedgerow and ruderal-forest species:

nearest_species(emb, "Robinia pseudoacacia")
                species  similarity
     Euonymus europaeus       0.770
         Sambucus nigra       0.715
           Prunus avium       0.710
         Acer campestre       0.710
          Rubus caesius       0.705

Solidago gigantea and Impatiens glandulifera are two riverbank invaders, and their neighbours are nearly the same floodplain species: native willows, other neophytes and tall riparian herbs.

nearest_species(emb, "Solidago gigantea")
                species  similarity
        Humulus lupulus       0.838
           Acer negundo       0.810
             Salix alba       0.801
    Echinocystis lobata       0.778
    Solidago canadensis       0.772

nearest_species(emb, "Impatiens glandulifera")
                species  similarity
        Carduus crispus       0.857
           Salix euxina       0.852
             Salix alba       0.839
        Humulus lupulus       0.823
    Echinocystis lobata       0.807

These results come from European Vegetation Archive (EVA) data, a database available on request. specvec ships no vegetation data. Compare embedding methods on your own data runs the workflow on simulated plots and shows how to map an EVA export onto specvec().

Comparing embedding methods

compare_embeddings() scores the registered methods on held-out co-occurrence recovery and link prediction, and on habitat (EUNIS) or trait recovery where plot habitat labels or species traits are given:

compare_embeddings(x, methods = c("ca", "pmi", "abund_pmi", "glove"))

The criterion for a win is fixed before the scores are computed: a method beats the reference only if it exceeds it on both co-occurrence recovery and link prediction by more than two pooled standard deviations. On EVA samples of 10,000 and 200,000 plots this selects abund_pmi, and its lead over correspondence analysis is larger in the bigger sample. Methods: from plots to embeddings describes each method.

A method is a registered pair of a weighting and a factorization, so a new method is added with register_weighting(), register_factorization() or register_method(), as Extending specvec: weightings, factorizations, methods shows.
